name: Journaling / gratitude

lead: Journaling is regularly writing down thoughts or experiences; a gratitude journal lists things you are thankful for. People keep one during self-improvement to hold onto a steadier mood and a kinder self-view, which carries into how they present themselves.

The chain is reflective writing, then steadier mood and self-view, then more confident self-presentation. Research summarised on Wikipedia reports short-term mood gains, with longer-lasting effects for daily journals; writing three grateful items daily had some of the longest-lasting effects, strongest around six months. Benefits were greatest in people already inclined to gratitude. The studies measure well-being, not appearance.

paras: People write for a few minutes a day, often in the morning or evening, listing a few things they appreciate or noting how the day went. Some pair it with a progress log for gym, skincare or grooming routines so changes are easy to see over time.
No notable physical risks are reported. Studies measured effects over short periods, and the benefit was strongest in people already high in gratitude.

angle.text: Gratitude lists and journals are a reflective habit that steadies mood and self-image during self-improvement, which feeds into a more confident presentation. Small studies show modest well-being effects.

lead: Journaling is the habit of writing regularly about thoughts, events or feelings, and gratitude journaling is the variant in which the writer lists things they appreciate. The wiki lists it as a reflective lifestyle practice.

According to Wikipedia, gratitude exercises raised positive emotion immediately afterwards, and writing three grateful items daily had some of the longest-lasting effects in the studies described, with the benefit greatest around six months.[1] The same source notes that people already inclined to gratitude benefited most.[1]
No research found links journaling or gratitude practice to appearance or looks-related outcomes.

paras: Common formats are a daily list of things one is grateful for, a letter of thanks, or free-form reflective writing.[1]

Wikipedia summarises that grateful people report higher well-being, less depression and stress, and greater life satisfaction, while noting that effects varied by exercise, were measured over short periods and that cultural factors shape how gratitude is expressed.[1]

No studies found on journaling or gratitude for appearance-related outcomes. Studies of gratitude and related brief interventions in other settings include a pilot study of five-minute workplace interventions for nurse burnout[2] and an integrative review of gratitude interventions in people with diabetes.[3] These address different outcomes.
